title: An Open Source Program Office for New York City
subtitle: Executive summary

sections.title: Executive summary
sections.body_md: New York City agencies already rely on open source software, but no one in City government is responsible for it: there is no inventory of what agencies run, no review of the licenses that come with it, and no shared standard for the code the City writes. A small, permanent Open Source Program Office within OTI, with two or three staff, would move the City past this ad hoc stage, using an established framework for how these offices are organized and the public-domain tools the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services already uses to manage its code. The result would be safer software, less duplicate spending, and a clear record of what the City runs and owns.

sections.title: Context
sections.body_md:
City agencies already use open source software and build it into their own products and services. That is how most organizations start: internal, engineering-driven use.¹ What the City lacks is anyone responsible for it. No one keeps an inventory of what agencies run, reviews the license obligations that come with it, or sets shared standards for the code the City writes. New York previously tackled a similar issue in 2012 with Local Law 11 which requires every agency to publish its public data on a single portal, but this does not cover source code.²

In general, organizations, whether corporate, academic, or governmental, typically form an OSPO once they recognize they are consuming open source in this ad hoc manner, without documentation or support.³ New York is there now. Until someone owns that work, teams in separate agencies, on separate funding streams and contracts, keep solving the same problems, duplicating efforts and wasting valuable time and resources.⁴

- New York has written "open by default" into law once, for data. The Open Data Law covers data, not source code (NYC Open Data Law 2012)

sections.title: OSPO definition
sections.body_md: An open source program office (OSPO) serves as the center of competency for an organization's open source operations and structure. It is responsible for the open source code it uses and shares, and for defining and implementing strategies and policies to guide these efforts.⁵,⁶

notes.title: Notes
notes.body_md:
> Target: about 120 words.

- An OSPO is the unit an organization makes responsible for the open source it uses and the code it shares (Haddad 2022)
- It covers inbound code the organization depends on and outbound code it shares with others (Miller 2024)

cms.gov/digital-service/open-source-program-office

An open source program office (OSPO) serves as the center of competency for an organization's open source operations and structure. It is responsible for defining and implementing strategies and policies to guide these efforts. The function of the CMS OSPO is:

“Establish and maintain guidance, policies, practices, and talent pipelines that advance equity, build trust, and amplify impact across CMS, HHS, and Federal Open Source Ecosystems by working and sharing openly.”

sections.title: NYC's case
sections.body_md:
OSPOs have been studied and strategized extensively. One of the most comprehensive studies, the Linux Foundation's *A Deep Dive into Open Source Program Offices* by Ibrahim Haddad, outlines how an OSPO might be structured, the roles it needs, and the stages it moves through.⁷ Though largely focused on corporate OSPOs, its framework is applicable to NYC. 
In Haddad's maturity model, the City is at stage 0/4, ad hoc: agencies consistently use open source internally. Moving into stage one would mean committing to compliant licensing, educating developers, and tracking an inventory of the open source in use.⁸ Of Haddad's four strategy stages (consumer, participant, contributor, leader), the office would start as a consumer: using open source deliberately before producing it. That means:

- reviewing all open source activity, including license compliance
- a classification scheme for what to adopt: features, code maturity, the size and makeup of the developer community
- an inventory of open source across City government using software bills of materials (SBOMs), to find unmet license obligations and security vulnerabilities
- automated workflow software (metrics, security checks, repository scaffolding, CI checks on every deployment) that lets a small team cover many repositories.⁹

The Digital Service at the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) was the first to implement an OSPO in a US federal agency, and it maintains open source tools that help automate much of this work.¹⁰ These tools are discussed in the "How it would work" section.
Later, the OSPO could move into the participant stage: filing bug reports and contributing fixes to the projects the City depends on.¹¹

sections.title: The risks of staying ad hoc
sections.body_md:
An OSPO would make the open source the City already runs safer, cheaper and easier to account for. With an inventory and automated checks, the City would know where its code lives, what it depends on and which vulnerabilities affect it, so fixes go out faster.¹² Agencies could find and reuse what another agency has already built, instead of paying to build or buy it again.¹³ Code that is visible is also accountable: contractors' work can be reviewed, and a problem one user finds can be fixed for everyone.¹⁴ Keeping that knowledge in City hands lowers the continuity risk when teams and vendors move on.¹⁵ And open, public work gives early-career technologists real projects to learn from and show, which makes the office a recruiting tool for fellows, graduates and the firms that might contract with the City.¹⁶

Staying at the ad hoc stage carries the opposite risks: license obligations no one is tracking,¹⁷ vulnerabilities no one can locate quickly, and the same software paid for twice.¹⁸

notes.title: Notes
notes.body_md:
> Target: about 180 words. UCL splits this into benefits and the risks of not having an OSPO.

**Benefits of moving past the ad hoc stage**

- **Security:** after Log4J, CMS had to write to each contractor and take their word that the vulnerability wasn't in their software. With an inventory and automated checks, the agency knows where its code is and what it depends on, and fixes go out faster (Miller 2024)
- **Cost:** stop paying to build or buy the same thing twice (Miller 2024; DeCausemaker 2024a)
- **Accountability:** visibility into what contractors deliver; transparency forces accountability (DeCausemaker 2024a; Miller 2024)
- **Continuity:** lower continuity risk (DeCausemaker 2024a)
- **Talent:** an early-career pipeline and a recruiting tool (Miller 2024)

**Risks of staying ad hoc**

- License obligations no one is tracking (Haddad 2022)
- Vulnerabilities no one can locate quickly (Miller 2024)
- Duplicate spending across agencies (Miller 2024)

sections.title: How it would work
sections.body_md:
The office would follow the virtual model Haddad describes: a head of open source and a small core team inside OTI, working with staff across agencies who give part of their time, with spending running through OTI rather than a separate budget.¹⁹ Each agency would name an open source liaison, just as every agency already names an Open Data Coordinator under the Open Data Law.²⁰

Two or three permanent posts would cover the roles Haddad identifies.²¹ The first hire would head the office: someone with deep open source, technical and licensing knowledge who can also make the case for the work inside OTI. A senior engineer, ideally a full-stack generalist, would run the tooling. Compliance and documentation would fold into these two roles, with legal questions going to general counsel rather than an in-house lawyer.

Much of the day-to-day repository work is already automated by tools the CMS OSPO has placed in the public domain. Its five-tier maturity model could be copied exactly for use within OTI.²² Its repo-scaffolder works out which tier a project belongs in, generates the files that tier requires and includes a release checklist for each tier, while automated checks flag missing files and policies.²³ CMS's metrics site tracks the health of every repository.²⁴

The work would be phased. The first phase is Haddad's stage 1: an inventory of the open source in use and a review of its licensing. The second brings in maturity tiers, templates, automated checks, metrics and education for staff across agencies. Contributing back to the projects the City relies on would come later. All of it depends on an IT environment that allows collaboration with outside projects.²⁵

notes.title: Notes
notes.body_md:
> Target: about 250 words. UCL covers the plan, resources and organization here.

**Structure**

- A virtual OSPO: a head of open source and a small core team in OTI, working with staff across agencies who give part of their time (Haddad 2022)
- Spending comes through OTI rather than a separate budget (Haddad 2022)
- A liaison in each agency, on the model of the Open Data Coordinators every agency already names (NYC Open Data Law 2012)

**Staff (two or three permanent posts)**

- Head of the OSPO: the primary hire, with deep open source, technical and licensing knowledge; also the office's main advocate inside OTI (Haddad 2022)
- Senior engineer: a full-stack generalist who runs the tools
- Compliance and documentation folded into these roles; general counsel for legal questions, not in-house (Haddad 2022)

**Repository work, using CMS's public-domain tools**

- The five-tier repository maturity model, copied exactly for use within OTI (DeCausemaker 2024a)
- repo-scaffolder: templates for each tier's files, a release checklist per tier, and a script that works out a project's tier (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-c)
- Automated checks for missing files and policies (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-c; TODO Group n.d.)
- The CMS metrics site (Digital Service at CMS n.d.-a)

**Plan**

- Phase 1: inventory and licensing review, the stage 1 work
- Phase 2: maturity tiers, templates, automated checks, metrics and staff education across agencies
- Later: contributing back

sections.title: Measuring success
sections.body_md: The office would choose its measures with its champions in OTI, so that it tracks what decision-makers need to see.²⁶ Much of the evidence can be gathered automatically. CMS's public metrics site reports the basic health of every repository: commits, pull requests and issues, the number of contributors, how long it takes to respond to an issue and how long to merge a fix.²⁷ The OpenSSF Scorecard adds at least 12 security measures for each project.²⁸ Other outcomes would be counted by hand: repositories released, tools reused by a second agency, costs reduced, security risks mitigated and people hired.²⁹ The first inventory would set the baseline. Each year the office would publish a short public report on its progress, as the City already does for open data through the annual compliance plan required by Local Law 11.³⁰

notes.title: Notes
notes.body_md:
> Target: about 150 words.

- Measures chosen with the office's champions in OTI, to fit what they need to see: CMS's lead consulted the CIO and CISO on which metrics to prioritize (CHAOSS 2024)
- Repository health, pulled automatically by the CMS metrics site (Miller 2024; Digital Service at CMS n.d.-a):
  - commits, pull requests and issues
  - number of contributors
  - time to respond to issues
  - time to merge a fix
- Security: OpenSSF Scorecard results, 12+ security metrics per project (Miller 2024)
- Outcomes tracked by hand: repositories released, tools reused by a second agency (Miller 2024), costs reduced (DeCausemaker 2024b; CMS OSPO n.d.-i), risks mitigated (DeCausemaker 2024b), people hired (our own proposal, no public source yet)
- A yearly public report, on the model of the Open Data Law's annual compliance plan (NYC Open Data Law 2012)

sections.title: Mission and goals
sections.body_md:
**Mission:** to make the open source software New York City relies on known, secure and shared, so that it serves New Yorkers better and every public dollar spent on code goes further.³¹

**Goals:**

- Every City repository has a maturity tier and an owner.
- Every agency knows what open source it runs.
- No tool is bought or built twice without checking first.
